title: Canonicalize a/num to a*(temp_num)>>n for non-power-of-2 constant division.

timeline.body:
We want to use some cheaper instructions to implement a division operation, of which
the divisor is a constant but not a power of 2 one, instead of using "div" directly.
The main conversion theory is shown here:
"a/num -> a*(1/num) -> a*(temp_num)/2^n -> a*(temp_num)>>n".

I borrowed the existing algorithm from Hacker's Delight by Henry S. Warren, Jr, and
almost verbatim the codes from it with just translate the C codes to JAVA codes.

Here is two jmh performance results with -wi 10 -i 5:
```
             without this patch   with this patch   units
fasta              349.741             347.511       us/op
fastaredux         196.150             188.920       us/op
```

And here is a division unit test:
```
private final int func(int n, int[] arr) {
    int ret = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        int var = arr[i];
        ret += var / 139968;
    }
    return ret;
}
```
and its performance results with -wi 15 -i 10:
```
               without this patch   with this patch    units
divConst         8824705,725        7350144,387     us/op
```

timeline.body: At line 90, we have `long divisor = isDivisorPositive ? c : -c;`, is `Math.abs` necessary here? Also in the preceding line, divisor will be negative only if it is `MIN_VALUE`, is that what we want?

reply.body: Yes, you are right. `Math.abs` is not needed because we already have `long divisor = isDivisorPositive ? c : -c;`. I retain it here just because that I want to keep the codes same with the original Hack's Delight algorithm. I want to keep the algorithm's integrality.
I think the original algorithm accepts negative divisor and it is not necessary to perform `long divisor = isDivisorPositive ? c : -c` upon calling this method.

Is `(divisor >>> (size - 1))` attempting to fetch the sign? Then it should be 63 because divisor is already extended to 64-bit.

I think the problem could be the [negative magic number](https://github.com/oracle/graal/pull/896#discussion_r250083650) you were mentioning. My colleague @rschatz provides me a patch that adjusts the result accordingly. It does pass the aforementioned failing gate.
[Here](https://github.com/mur47x111/graal/commit/651397563009c94354792dda50cace5451b34ac2#diff-4f6bf62a8bac360a77465f3bdbc98b76) it is. If that is OK, I can take care of the changes.

I compared the generated codes with this patch and my one for the test:
`public static int intDivPositiveConstant(int val) {
        return val / 5;
  }`
The main instructions with this patch:
**smull    x0, x1, w0
 lsr    x0, x0, #32  
 lsr    w1, w1, #31    
 add    w0, w1, w0, asr #1**

And instructions with my:
**mul    x0, x1, x0  
 asr    x0, x0, #33  
 mov    w0, w0   
 sub    w0, w0, w1, asr #31**

Comparing the two patterns, the "mul" instruction has low time latency than "smull", and also the `mov    w0, w0` can be optimized in future. So I think if we can use "mul" while not "smull", the performance may be better.
Thanks for the feedback! I will use `mul` for 32-bits division then.
